To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the outdoor gamma radiation dose rates are mainly due to natural radionuclides, and that the exposure time to achieve a certain yearly effective radiation dose depends on the dose rate and on the gamma index of the material.
the absorbed dose rate in air is related to the gamma index of the materials, which in turn is related to their U, Th, K content.
the absorbed dose rate in outdoor environments depends on the content of natural radioisotopes in soils, rocks, and building materials.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the assessment of the radiological hazards related with outdoor gamma radiation in terms of dose rate and exposure time.
the assessment of the hazard related to the outdoor radiation dose rate.

the evaluation of outdoor gamma radiation hazards and the development of simple methods for assessing the exposure time necessary to reach a certain yearly effective radiation dose in outdoor environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dose rate is not a good indicator of the hazard, but the effective dose rate is a better indicator.
the outdoor absorbed dose rate is a good parameter to be used in risk assessment studies.
the absorbed dose rate in outdoor environments, in the case of the materials studied here, is related to the gamma index of the materials and to their content in K, U, and Th.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dose rate in outdoor environments depends not only on the content of the radioisotopes in the rocks, but also on the type of the rocks, their texture, and their thickness.
a dose rate of 1 mGy/year is equivalent to 10 years of exposure to an outdoor gamma index of 0.2.
a high gamma index of rocks is a good indicator for high absorbed dose rate values.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the absorbed dose rate in outdoor environments is a function of the exposure time, the effective dose, and the gamma index, which is related to the radioisotopes content.
, for a given yearly effective dose, the time spent outdoors is inversely related to the dose rate.
, in general, the outdoor dose rate is low enough that a person would have to remain exposed for a long time to reach a yearly effective dose of 1 mSv.
